goals.goal: tokio vs async-std: which one is still maintained and what differs?

nuggets.text: The async-std README states that async-std has been discontinued.
The async-std README recommends that users switch to smol instead.
async-std is described as providing an async version of the Rust standard library (std) with the same interfaces.
Tokio provides a multithreaded, work-stealing based task scheduler.
Tokio's current MSRV (minimum supported Rust version) is 1.85, under a rolling policy of at least 6 months.
smol is described as a small and fast async runtime, and tokio-based libraries can be used with it via the async-compat adapter.

goals.goal: Rust Rc vs Arc: when should I use each?

nuggets.text: Rc is a single-threaded reference-counting pointer.
Arc is a thread-safe reference-counting pointer; its name stands for Atomically Reference Counted.
Arc uses atomic operations for its reference counting, which are more expensive than ordinary memory accesses.
The docs recommend Rc<T> for lower overhead when reference-counted allocations are not shared between threads.
Rc is !Send and !Sync, so the compiler rejects attempts to send an Rc between threads.
Arc<T> implements Send and Sync only if T implements Send and Sync.

goals.goal: PostgreSQL json vs jsonb: what are the differences?

nuggets.text: The json type stores an exact copy of the input text, which processing functions must reparse on each execution.
jsonb is stored in a decomposed binary format, making it slightly slower to input but significantly faster to process.
jsonb supports indexing, which the docs call a significant advantage.
json preserves semantically-insignificant white space and the order of object keys; jsonb does not preserve white space or key order.
jsonb does not keep duplicate object keys; if duplicates are given in the input, only the last value is kept.
The docs say most applications should prefer storing JSON data as jsonb unless they have specialized needs such as legacy assumptions about key ordering.

goals.goal: HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: what differs in the transport and header compression?

nuggets.text: HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics over the QUIC transport protocol, while HTTP/2 has been used primarily with TLS over TCP.
HTTP/3 replaces HTTP/2's HPACK header compression with QPACK.
QPACK uses separate unidirectional streams to modify and track field table state.
HTTP/3 clients select the protocol via the "h3" ALPN token in the TLS handshake, or discover it via Alt-Svc.
If UDP is blocked and a QUIC connection fails, HTTP/3 clients SHOULD attempt a TCP-based version of HTTP.
HTTP/2 uses binary message framing and allows multiple concurrent exchanges interleaved on the same connection.

goals.goal: git merge vs git rebase: how do they integrate branches and when should I avoid rebase?

nuggets.text: git merge performs a three-way merge using the two branch-tip snapshots and their common ancestor.
A merge commit is special in that it has more than one parent.
If the branch being merged is directly ahead of the current commit, git merge just moves the pointer forward (a fast-forward).
git rebase takes the changes committed on one branch and replays them on top of another branch.
Rebasing produces a linear-looking history, as if all the work happened in series.
Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on.

goals.goal: Python list vs tuple: mutability and typical use

nuggets.text: Tuples are immutable; assigning to an item raises TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment.
Lists are mutable.
Tuples usually contain a heterogeneous sequence of elements accessed via unpacking or indexing.
List elements are usually homogeneous and accessed by iterating over the list.
A tuple can contain mutable objects, such as lists.
A tuple is created by comma-separated values (tuple packing), e.g. t = 12345, 54321, 'hello!'.

goals.goal: Rust HashMap vs BTreeMap: ordering, key requirements and when to pick which

nuggets.text: HashMap iterates its keys and entries in arbitrary order.
HashMap keys must implement the Eq and Hash traits.
HashMap's hash table is a Rust port of Google's SwissTable.
HashMap's default hashing algorithm is currently SipHash 1-3, though this is subject to change.
BTreeMap is an ordered map based on a B-Tree that stores entries in key order, so keys must implement Ord.
The std::collections guide says to use a BTreeMap when you want a map sorted by its keys or to get a range of entries on demand.

goals.goal: Rust Mutex vs RwLock: differences in locking and poisoning

nuggets.text: An RwLock allows a number of readers or at most one writer at any point in time.
A Mutex does not distinguish between readers and writers that acquire the lock.
RwLock does not guarantee any particular priority policy; it depends on the underlying operating system's implementation.
A Mutex becomes poisoned if the thread holding it panics, and lock and try_lock then return a Result indicating whether it is poisoned.
Mutex<T> is Sync when T: Send, while RwLock<T> is Sync only when T: Send + Sync.
